analysis.one_liner: Expands the child tax credit, adds paid parental leave drawn from Social Security, and funds anti-abortion pregnancy support.
analysis.headline: Rubio's Providing for Life Act never got a committee or floor vote in the 118th Congress; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee for two years with one cosponsor until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill combines a large package of family tax and benefit provisions with an anti-abortion agenda. It would raise the child tax credit to $3,500 per child ($4,500 for children under six), make the adoption credit refundable, let new parents draw up to three months of paid leave from Social Security, and extend WIC postpartum eligibility to two years. At the same time, it would fund pregnancy resource centers that do not provide abortion, require colleges to tell pregnant students about resources that exclude abortion, build a federal "life.gov" site steering women away from abortion providers, and guarantee religious organizations equal access to federal social-service contracts. It died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, low- and middle-income parents would get a bigger child tax credit, adoptive parents a refundable credit, new parents up to three months of paid leave (which they must later repay), postpartum mothers an extra year of WIC, and pregnant students and expectant mothers new campus and federal resources — all of which exclude abortion providers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents with young children; mothers keeping pregnancies

how_it_helps.text: The child tax credit would rise to $3,500 per child, $4,500 for children under six, with the income phaseout threshold set at $400,000 for joint returns.
The adoption tax credit would become refundable, meaning families who owe little tax could still receive its full value.
Parents with enough Social Security work credits could draw a monthly payment for up to three months after a birth or adoption, with the amount based on their projected Social Security benefit.
Postpartum eligibility under WIC would extend from one year to two, and fathers could be ordered to cover at least half of a mother's out-of-pocket pregnancy and delivery costs.
Noncustodial parents behind on child support would be prioritized for $100 million in workforce-training grants, and SNAP recipients would be required to cooperate with child-support agencies.
Federal grants would flow to community maternal-mentoring programs and to pregnancy resource centers that do not provide abortions, and a new life.gov website would list resources for pregnant women.
Public colleges would have to inform students of rights and accommodations for pregnant students, with the information required to exclude abortion services.

analysis.who_pays: The credits would cost the Treasury, funded in part by eliminating the federal deduction for state and local taxes — a tax increase concentrated on itemizers in high-tax states. Parental leave would be fronted by the Social Security trust fund and repaid by recipients through smaller retirement checks or a later retirement age. Abortion providers and the women who seek their services would be excluded from federally funded information and referral systems.

drawbacks.text: The paid leave is not free money: every recipient must repay the full cost of the benefit later, either through deductions from their future Social Security retirement checks (up to the first 60 payments) or by electing a later retirement age, with fraud penalties of up to $7,500 per violation.

The bill eliminates the federal deduction for state and local taxes, which would raise federal income taxes on households that itemize — a cost that falls hardest on middle- and upper-middle-income families in states with higher taxes.

The pregnancy-resource provisions are one-sided: college notices, the life.gov website, and grant eligibility all exclude abortion providers and organizations that counsel in favor of abortion, and a government portal would list "abortion risks" without the excluded providers' services as alternatives.

The religious-organizations section would let faith-based groups contract for federally funded social services while retaining religious hiring exemptions and limiting federal audits to segregated accounts holding federal money.

An unborn child could be claimed as a qualifying child for the prior tax year if a Social Security number is issued before birth, embedding a particular legal definition of personhood into the tax code.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family provisions are real and sizable for ordinary parents — a larger child tax credit and refundable adoption credit would put cash in households that need it, and two years of WIC postpartum is a concrete improvement. But the leave benefit is a loan against your own future retirement rather than new money, the SALT repeal shifts part of the cost onto taxpayers in high-tax states, and roughly half the bill is dedicated to steering women away from abortion through government-funded channels while excluding providers of that care from every resource it creates. Supporters would call it pro-family and pro-life; critics would call it an abortion-restriction vehicle wrapped around tax credits. Both descriptions fit the text.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2023 and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the Providing for Life Act of 2023 in the Senate on January 25, 2023.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action ever appears in its history.
One Republican senator cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

The bill would have raised the child tax credit to $3,500 per child, created paid parental leave drawn from Social Security, extended WIC postpartum benefits to two years, and funded pregnancy resource centers and a life.gov information portal that exclude abortion providers.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still pending in committee, so every provision expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained enactment: families got no expanded credit or leave, and the anti-abortion funding and information provisions never took effect. Taxpayers in high-tax states also avoided the bill's repeal of the state and local tax deduction, and abortion providers avoided new exclusions from federal resources.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no one gained enactment

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and designed it as a combined family-tax-credit and anti-abortion package.

for.name: 1 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for the remainder of the 118th Congress — no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the party split was never tested; the sponsor and the bill's single cosponsor were both Republicans, and no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: The bill would create federal grants and life.gov listings reserved for centers that do not provide or refer for abortion, giving this sector public funding and government referrals for the first time at this scale. Women who choose to continue a pregnancy would gain free material and counseling services; women seeking abortion would be steered away from those providers.

An 'equal treatment' section would guarantee faith-based groups access to federal social-service funding on the same basis as secular providers while preserving religious hiring exemptions and limiting federal audits to segregated federal-funds accounts. This would open a broad federal funding channel to religious providers; beneficiaries who object to a provider's religious character would be entitled to a referral elsewhere.

The bill defines any entity that performs, induces, or counsels for abortion as a 'prohibited entity' barred from the new grants, and excludes abortion services from college notices and the life.gov portal. Providers and the women who would use their services both lose access to the federally funded resource system this bill builds.

Eliminating the federal deduction for state and local taxes would raise these households' federal taxes, providing a partial offset for the expanded child tax credit. Their loss helps fund the family benefits.

Public institutions would face new reporting duties — campus-wide notices of pregnant students' rights, student surveys, and annual reports to Congress — with no new funding attached. Pregnant students would gain information and a complaint protocol, though the required notices must exclude abortion services.
